text: When you type a message to an AI, you use words, and it responds with words.
Underneath, the system splits your text into small pieces, called tokens.
Each token is assigned an embedding, a row of numbers that represents its starting meaning.
Since the AI only works with these numbers, it relies on the surrounding words to figure out the exact meaning of every token.
There are two problems this context has to solve.
The first is words with multiple meanings.
In the sentence, please turn on the light, the word refers to brightness.
The empty suitcase felt light means not heavy.
For pronouns, in the cat was thirsty, so it drank the milk, it is the cat.
In the milk was fresh, so the cat drank it, it points to the milk.
Context determines which meaning fits.
While our brains resolve these meanings instantly, earlier AI struggled because it read text in a strict sequence, one word at a time.
The AI reads, the tired cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm.
Eventually, it reaches the sentence, it soon fell asleep.
By the time the AI reaches the word it, the word cat is far back in the sequence, with several other words now sitting between them.
Earlier AI often struggled to keep that connection, especially in longer passages.
In 2017, researchers at Google published, Attention is All You Need.
This introduced the transformer architecture, the T in chat GPT.
The transformer can process the tokens in your message in parallel.
This layout illustrates how the complete message arrives all at once.
Every word in the sequence is visible to the system at the exact same time.
Now, the token, it, draws directly on the token, cat.
The intervening words no longer act as a barrier.
Reading everything at once is only the start.
The AI must still identify which specific words actually matter, so it can update the numbers for each token.
This process involves two steps.
First, through attention, the model weighs information from relevant words and blends it into the token's numbers.
Then, through transformation, the model uses learned patterns to further process those blended numbers, refining the token's meaning.
Attention and transformation work together to build meaning from context.
It's important to note that the model itself isn't learning while it reads your prompt.
The model's learned weights stay fixed.
Only the row of numbers representing the tokens in your current message are being updated.
In our examples, please turn on the light, turn on tells the AI light means brightness.
The empty suitcase felt light means not heavy.
The word empty shifts those exact same starting numbers to represent a lack of weight.
For pronouns, in the cat was thirsty, so it drank the milk, it is the cat.
In the milk was fresh, so the cat drank it, it points to the milk.
Attention and transformation help AI work out which meaning fits.
By identifying these connections across the whole sentence, the transformer can resolve more than just simple nouns.
It uses these same relationship mapping tools to interpret the intent behind sarcasm, idioms, or even placeholder words like the it in It Was a Cold Day.
However, reading everything at once creates a problem that sequential reading never had.
The model loses the sense of word order.
Consider Dog Bites Man versus Man Bites Dog.
They use the exact same tokens.
Without position information, the words just float scattered and the model can't tell which event actually happened.
To fix this, the system uses position stamps to preserve the original sequence of the words.
Positional encoding tells the transformer where every token belongs.
Attention is all you need.
AI uses relationships between words to help interpret your message.
